title: Al-'Alaq: the one who forbids
hook: the man who forbids a servant to pray, and the command to bow and draw near (96:9–19)
tomorrow: At-Tin: the fig and the olive

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-'Alaq, the first words in the cave: read. Your line was taught by the pen. Did you write one line by hand, and what did you write? Day one hundred eighty-two.

The Ka'bah in Mecca, in the early years. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is praying there, in the open, bowing, then putting his forehead on the ground. A powerful man of Quraysh is watching, and he's furious. He tells his friends: if I see Muhammad with his face in the dust again, I'll step on his neck. Someone who wants to stop another person from praying. The rest of Surah al-'Alaq, after the first five verses, is about this man, and about what the one praying should do. Today: Al-'Alaq, the one who forbids.
screen: `PRAYING IN THE OPEN.` → `I'LL STEP ON HIS NECK.` → `WHAT SHOULD THE ONE PRAYING DO?`

segments.voice: The surah turns from the pen to a warning: truly, the human being oversteps when he sees himself as self-sufficient. Then: have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays? The man isn't named in the surah. Commentators, and a hadith in Sahih Muslim, identify him as Abu Jahl, a leading opponent of the Prophet in Mecca. The hadith says he came forward to carry out his threat, and then suddenly drew back, shielding himself with his hands. Asked why, he said he'd seen between himself and the Prophet a trench of fire, and terror, and wings. The surah asks him questions: what if the one praying is rightly guided? What if he commands goodness? Doesn't he know that Allah sees? And then the last verse, which tells the one praying what to do. In Pickthall's translation: Nay! Obey not thou him. But prostrate thyself, and draw near unto Allah. Not fight him. Not argue. Not hide. Bow down, and come closer. It's counted among the verses of prostration, though the schools of law differ on it. And it lines up with a hadith in Muslim: the closest a servant is to his Lord is while in prostration. So the lowest position of the body is the nearest point to Allah. The man who wanted to push a face into the dust didn't understand: that's exactly where the nearness is. And that closes a week that began with the quake and an atom of good, and moved through the earth's report, the clear proof, sincerity, the Night of Power, and now the cave and its first surah, whole.
screen: `HE SEES HIMSELF AS SELF-SUFFICIENT.` · `THE ONE WHO FORBIDS PRAYER.` · `OBEY NOT THOU HIM.` · `CLOSEST IN PROSTRATION.` · then, large: `BOW AND DRAW NEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you pray, you can make one prostration now, forehead to the ground, and stay there a few breaths longer than usual, drawing near. If you don't, try something like it: lower your head, gently, toward your knees or your hands, and let your whole body get small and still. Notice what it feels like to go low on purpose. Nothing to prove down there. The bell holds the time.
Al-'Alaq. The clinging thing, and the surah that ends: don't obey the one who forbids; bow down, and draw near. Today's word.
Your line: bow and draw near. When someone tries to shame you out of what you value today, don't fight it. Go lower, and closer. Day one hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: When Muslims recite or hear 96:19 many perform a prostration of recitation (sajdat al-tilawah); in the daily prayers, the prostration is often called the moment of greatest nearness to Allah.

original.note: Arabic: and draw near; the last word of Surah 96.

what it means: the answer to someone who forbids prayer is to bow lower and come closer.
what a scholar hears: 96:6–7 on self-sufficiency and transgression; Muslim 2797 for Abu Jahl; Muslim 482 on nearness in prostration; 96:19 is among the prostration verses.

Prostration at 96:19: the Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools count it; the Maliki school traditionally does not. The script says 'Muslims traditionally prostrate'; a Keeper may want to add the difference.
